Went To China To Conquer America: Unearthed Rushes In New Feature Doc Give Fresh Perspectives On A Pop History Moment ‘Happy Old Year,’ From ‘I’m Still Here’ Author Marcelo Rubens Paiva, Being Adapted As Netflix Series View All August 3, 2026 5:02am Kaufman Astoria Studios Courtesy EXCLUSIVE: Shadowbox Studios has taken on management of Kaufman Astoria Studios in New York. The 500,000 square-foot campus in Astoria, Queens, is an historic studio facility where classic film and TV hits including Goodfellas and Sesame Street filmed, as well as contemporary shows including Succession and Just Like That , and movies including The Devil Wears Prada 2 . Today, the landmark studio comprises 11 soundstages and 325,000 square-feet of office and production support space. Shadowbox takes on management of Kaufman Astoria after a tumultuous period at the studios. In April, Deutsche Bank filed a foreclosure complaint against Kaufman Astoria Studios and its then owner Hackman Capital Partners, alleging a default on a $340 million loan that was due to be paid last fall. It starts managing the studios, which were originally built in the 1920s as the home of Paramount Pictures, from today. “We want to welcome producers to this incredible studio to be enriched by its history and the storytellers that have come before them at the same time as offering a top-tier customer service to meet the demands of today’s production needs,” said Mike Mosallam , Chief Operating Officer, Shadowbox Studios. He added: “Our team is looking forward to working with the on-lot staff to thoughtfully integrate the Shadowbox Studios standards of excellence. Whatever the production, we will work in partnership to make it seamless.” Shadowbox already runs studios in the U.S. and internationally. Shadowbox Atlanta is a nine-soundstage complex that has been home to Jumanji and Godzilla: King of Monsters . In the UK, there is Shadowbox Shinfield, an 18-soundstage facility that has played host to Star Wars: The Acolyte and Ghostbusters: Frozen Empire . It is currently developing a 10-soundstage complex in Queensland, Australia. title: Christopher Nolan China Interview Goes Viral Over Frank Views on Critics, Christian Themes in ‘The Odyssey,’ Being a “Bard for a Civilization at Dusk”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abid Rahman Plus Icon Abid Rahman International Editor, Digital gentlemanabroad Follow Sign Up View All August 3, 2026 4:55am Christopher Nolan Josh Telles/PMC Despite The Odyssey giving up the throne to Spider-Man: Brand New Day at the box office, Christopher Nolan continues to make news, this time for a press tour interview he did in China that got deeply philosophical about art, history, storytelling, modern film criticism, and the appearance of Christian conceptions of atonement in his soon-to-be billion-dollar blockbuster. Speaking to Chinese podcaster and political philosophy lecturer Zhong Shu in Beijing, which first appeared on China’s Bilibili video platform, the British filmmaker has something of a hard break from the usual interviews he’s done on The Odyssey’s globe-spanning press tour. There were no games, no soft-ball or rushed questions about his favorite moments from the production or anecdotes about the actors, instead Zhong’s interview was one of the rare ones where the filmmaker was probed about his personal philosophy and worldview and how that informed the making of The Odyssey . Related Stories Movies Sarajevo Unveils Open Air Program, Including Diego Luna's 'Ashes,' 'Minotaur' and 'No Good Men' Movies In 'Donkey Princess,' a Young Royal Travels Through Worlds - and Film Genres - in Search of Love (Exclusive Trailer) As such, it was perhaps no surprise that the interview has gone viral as it gave us a fascinating insight into the thinking of arguably the world’s most popular filmmaker at the peak of his powers. Here are some key takeaways and highlights. “Bard of a civilization at dusk.” Zhong began the interview, which was conducted in English, by describing Nolan as a bard of the modern age, as Homer was a bard of Ancient Greece and then describing the latter’s poem as a celebration of war and victory, whereas Nolan’s adaptation of The Odyssey is most certainly the oppposite, reflecting more the current day. Zhong followed up by asking the director, due to the tone of his film, whether he was a “bard of a civilization at dusk?” “I think that’s a really interesting point, a really interesting question,” Nolan said with a laugh. “I mean underlying the main part of the point is this 400-year-or-so gap between the events that Homer is describing when Homer’s story was written down, or first received by readers and audiences. That’s a pretty interesting gap, and for me, I don’t think I’m completely at odds with the way Homer is telling the story. When you look at it from a sort of historical perspective and the reason is — and what I got interested in as I adapted it — is that Homer’s writing about an era before his, he’s writing about an era hundreds of years before. His audience viewed it as being more advanced than theirs. So they were a civilization on the rise, but they were trying to get back to where they had been 400 years before. So that idea of a cycle, that idea of, as you say, a civilization at dusk. I think it’s there in the poem, it’s subtle. But when you look at the history as well… when they would unearth these walls of old palaces that were crumbled, they called them Cyclopian walls because they thought only a giant could have built such grand walls. They had this idea of the greatness of this past civilization. And so I became interested by that collapse, what they call the catastrophe, the Bronze Age collapse. What happens between the events of the Trojan War and Homer.” He added, “I think [those themes are] something that from a modern perspective is frightening and interesting and I think for me it partly comes out of having worked on Oppenheimer before this, which is very much a film about the end of the world, about the end of and collapse of civilization, ultimately. So I think yeah I definitely carried that sensibility into this adaptation of The Odyssey .” Concepts of atonement. Zhong then moved on to the concept of “atonement” in Nolan’s film, saying that such a concept doesn’t exist in Ancient Greek culture, or language, or in Homer’s poem. She asked directly whether the filmmaker had “Christianized The Odyssey ” and further why atonement was so important in the film. “I wasn’t too conscious of how I was approaching it philosophically other than I really honed in on the idea of what’s termed ‘xenia,’ said Nolan. “In the film we call it Zeus’s Law for simplicity, but it’s that idea of mutual respect – that I treat you the way I want to be treated. And in their theology it’s because you might be a god in disguise. I really drilled down on that, and I started to realize that for me a lot of what’s interesting about the interaction of history and mythology is this idea of the ‘sea peoples’, the idea of the people from the sea who were thought to have precipitated the Bronze Age collapse. It’s one of the great mysteries of history: who were they? But the idea that really a violation of xenia, a violation of Zeus’ Law — which is what the suitors are doing in the palace — that really is the [breaking] of Zeus’ Law that is causing this difficulty and this damage. “I think the idea of atonement in a way is what we bring as viewers to the story,” Nolan added. “I don’t know whether there really is atonement in the film, or whether we just feel that catharsis or that’s the process we’re seeing in the final meeting that we’ve waited for between Odysseus and Penelope. But I think in a way we maybe bringing our more modern sensibility to that. Insofar as [atonement is] there, it’s not a deliberate attempt to Christianize it, but it’s an outgrowth or it’s a natural conclusion of burrowing in on this philosophical idea of what happens when you break Zeus’ Law.” Modern film criticism, storytelling and tropes. Circling back to Homer’s poem, and how it celebrates the great men of history, Zhong then probed Nolan on whether his adaptation “apologizes” for this sense of greatness to suit modern sensibilities. “Is [ The Odyssey ] a story of apology that demands repentance, and reflection and self-criticism?, asked Zhong. I think that when you’re talking about storytelling, you’re always in conversation with the expectations of the audience,” Nolan began his considered reply. “So, it really is an energy that’s brought from the audience as well as an energy that’s put forward from the story itself. When you’re characterizing somebody, and the trite version of this, or the criticism that is often leveled at movies in general, is, ‘oh, the character has to be made sympathetic’ — so the character is manipulated in different ways or changed in different ways. And that’s a fundamental flaw of film criticism in a way, or storytelling criticism, because to be able to identify the mechanism does not invalidate the mechanism. And that’s a real problem in criticism today because people have this idea that: because I can understand why the story affects me the way it is, therefore, it didn’t work. That’s not how storytelling works. When we create a heroic figure in a story as storytellers, we have to be mindful of the energy that the audience brings to that story and the interaction between our intention and the way the audience receives that. And the fact that mechanism is identifiable to people doesn’t invalidate it. Part of that mechanism is saying, ‘are we going to treat greatness as an absolute or coming from a democratic or… more idealized philosophical state that we live in, in today’s world, where we want to view people as equal. Do we have to apologize for that greatness? And the answer is yes, we do, or the audience rejects the greatness, and that is part of the mechanism. Once again, the fact that the mechanism is identifiable doesn’t mean that it’s invalid or shouldn’t be used.” Later in the interview Nolan returns to his views of modern “amateur” film criticism. “When I was talking about film criticism, I was talking more about amateur film criticism than professional film criticism, because professional film criticism tends to understand the necessity for the mechanisms. So you’re looking at a lingua frana of storytelling created by Hollywood for the last 100 years that is very effectively universal and so it is its own language, and that language is understood by people all over the world, which is what’s incredible about it. And it is a very accessible modern language of storytelling and it has certain rules. It has conventions, you can break those conventions, you can bend them. You can move them, but you have to be aware of them the whole time. As I say, I’m thinking more of amateur criticism when I say that people who, because they feel they’ve identified the mechanism, they feel that it invalidates it. That can be true of certain elements and film grammar, and film language evolves with that. “So when a trope becomes too familiar to an audience, then it has to be changed. But we do, as filmmakers, avail ourselves of that common language. We build on that understanding that our audience has seen many films. And that they understand that language. So, you’re playing with that language. It’s the language of genre. It’s the language of audience sympathy. It’s the language of clarity and of narrative direction and how you guide people through a story.” Nolan then linked his point about “mechanisms” to his film Memento . “You can’t completely have a tabula rasa; you can’t throw everything away. You have to make your choices in terms of ‘how am I orienting the story?’ So for example, one of my first films, Memento , was a story that I structured in reverse chronologically. But what I retained was a very clear and simple three-act structure. So the structure of the film as it’s received by the audience is very very conventional. But the chronology is unconventional. And so those are the choices you make. That’s one example where you say, ‘Okay, I need this to be extremely familiar underneath so that I can change what’s on the surface.’ And that’s a continual mechanism that’s evolving.” THR

title: ‘Where Is Austin Tice?’: BBC & NPR Team On Podcast Unravelling The Story Of Journalist Who Disappeared In Syria In 2012
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Opens To $355 Million U.S. & $927M Worldwide, Second Best Start Of All Time At Box Office Read the full story By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max International Insider: Netflix’s $500M Zombie Gamble; The New Scottish Fest; Ngozi Onwurah On ‘Welcome II The Terrordome’ Alan Cumming-Backed Block The Merger Submits Evidence To UK Culture Sec; Argues WarnerMount Will “Directly Impact UK Documentarians’ Ability To Tell Diverse Stories” FIFA Set To Lose Vote Over Controversial Private Investment Plan After Europe, Asia & Americas Reject Proposal View All August 3, 2026 4:00am BBC EXCLUSIVE: The BBC and NPR are teaming on a podcast about kidnapped American journalist Austin Tice . Josh Baker ’s Where is Austin Tice? sets out to answer questions in real time about the man who many consider to be the longest captive American journalist in history. The podcast, a rare co-pro between the BBC and NPR, will be on NPR’s Embedded feed from September 8 and will simultaneously comprise the third season of Baker’s I’m Not a Monster series for BBC Sounds and World Service. It will be hosted by Baker and investigative journalist Sara Obeidat. Related Stories News Jared Leto Allegations Are "Bellwether" Moment For MeToo In Hollywood, Says Producer Behind Explosive BBC Documentary Casting Claire Foy & Matthew Macfadyen To Lead David Nicholls Novel Adaptation 'You Are Here' For BBC & Starz Tice disappeared in Syria more than a decade ago and remains one of the biggest missing person cases of our time. His mother Debra insists her son is alive and has led a tireless campaign to bring him home — a campaign that continues to this day. He is thought to have been kidnapped by Syria’s regime led by the now-deposed Bashar al-Assad, making him the longest captive American journalist in history. Baker and Obeidat penned a BBC News investigation on the website last year that confirmed he was imprisoned by the Assad regime. Watch on Deadline The pod retraces Tice’s journey, allowing the audience to experience the investigation as it unfolds. It differs from the previous two seasons of I’m Not a Monster in that those cases were not unravelling in real time. The first series explored America’s Sam Sally, a mother who entered ISIS territory with her husband and children, and the second Shamima Begum, who joined ISIS as a teenager before trying to regain her British citizenship. Both have won numerous awards. “It is rare in journalism to have the chance to do work that might offer something tangible to a family while also showing the stark reality of the Syrian regime’s brutal dictatorship,” said Baker. “That possibility has driven us throughout — alongside a responsibility to the Syrians who trusted us with their stories and are still searching for answers about their own missing relatives.” Embedded senior supervising editor Katie Simon added: “When Josh and Sara first came to us with this story, we knew it was a rare opportunity to showcase immersive reporting about one of the most secretive regimes. The Austin Tice story gives us the chance to step into a once-hidden Syrian prison system and begin to piece together a play-by-play of Austin’s timeline from the moment he goes missing. It’s also a chance for two public media powerhouses to come together and make something new and meaningful in longform narrative journalism.” The podcast is written, showrun and presented by Baker and investigated and produced with Obeidat. It is series-produced by Simon Maybin and produced by Lucy Burns, with Clare Fordham as series editor for BBC News Long Form Audio. It was commissioned by Daniel Clarke for BBC Radio 4 and BBC Sounds. At NPR, the podcast was edited by Robert Little, who leads NPR’s Investigations team and Embedded ’s showrunner Simon. It was produced by Monika Evstatieva. The EP for Embedded is Irene Noguchi. BBC Studios is distributing the series. title: Sarajevo Unveils Open Air Program, Including Diego Luna’s ‘Ashes,’ ‘Minotaur’ and ‘No Good Men’
full_text: × Skip to main content By Lily Ford Plus Icon Lily Ford @lilyfordtweets Follow Sign Up View All August 3, 2026 3:48am 'Minotaur' Cannes Film Festival Sarajevo Film Festival has unveiled its Open Air program, with films such as the Cannes-premiering Minotaur and Diego Luna ‘s Ashes set to screen at the fest’s largest venue, the Coca-Cola Open Air Cinema. Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , starring Hanns Zischler and Sandra Hüller, will open the section at the Bosnian film festival, with Danis Tanović’s 2001 film No Man’s Land set to close it. The movie takes place in 1993, during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. By a twist of fate, Čiki, a soldier in the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, finds himself trapped in the same trench as Nino, a Bosnian Serb soldier. Related Stories Movies In 'Donkey Princess,' a Young Royal Travels Through Worlds - and Film Genres - in Search of Love (Exclusive Trailer) Movies Woody Harrelson to Receive Honorary Heart of Sarajevo at Bosnian Film Festival Also premiering in the program is Luna’s film about two siblings forced to leave Mexico and head to Madrid to reunite with their mother, who had left a few years earlier to chase a better future. When they arrive, however, the bitter, suffocating reality that awaits them proves far harsher than imagined. Luna spoke to The Hollywood Reporter at Cannes about the making of the film and why it was a deeply personal project. Also screening is Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur , another feature from Cannes, following a successful company director called Gleb , who finds himself under siege from mounting corporate pressures and an increasingly unstable world. The collapse of his carefully ordered life accelerates towards violence. The Berlinale opener No Good Men from Shahrbanoo Sadat is also set for a Sarajevo premiere. It focuses on Naru, the only camerawoman at Kabul’s main TV station, who struggles to keep custody of her three-year-old son after leaving her husband, a serial cheater. Convinced no good men exist in her country, Naru is caught off guard when Qodrat, Kabul TV’s most respected journalist, gives her a career opportunity. Among other movies premiering in this section are Annemarie Jacir’s Palestine 36 , Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved , and Michael Winterbottom’s 1997 film Welcome to Sarajevo , in honor of the recently announced Honorary Heart of Sarajevo recipient Woody Harrelson . Also on Monday, the Sarajevo Film Festival unveiled its Open Air Premiere program, which brings together the most anticipated new films from the region of the former Yugoslavia. These movies are screened at UNIQA Open Air Cinema Stari Grad, and the best film — selected by audiences — will receive the Prix Cineplexx. Among the features in this selection are Miroslav Terzić’s 3 Weeks After , Miha Hočevar’s Hidden People , and Marijana Jankovic’s Home . Igor Jelinović’s Honey Bunny will screen, as will Darko Štante’s The Lost Son , Predrag Ličina’s The Virus of Pathological Kindness , and Hari Šečić’s The Widower , about a 62-year-old electrician who was raised and lives in a patriarchal society. When his daily routine changes after the sudden death of his wife, Enisa, Mirsad tries to get used to a life without her and soon realizes that he took her for granted. The 32nd Sarajevo Film Festival will take place Aug. 14-21. THR

title: CBS News Correspondent Trevor Phillips Says Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss ‘Will Either Change the World or Crash and Burn’

He will also join “60 Minutes.” A veteran writer and broadcaster as well as a former politician, Phillips was previously chair of the U.K.’s Equality and Human Rights Commission and in 2022 was knighted for his services to equality and human rights . Popular on Variety He is set to move across the pond this summer to take up the new role at CBS. “You know, I’m 72. It’s a great adventure,” he said of Weiss’s offer. “And who turns down adventures if someone is willing to take a chance on you?” To mark the move, Phillips gave a wide-ranging interview to the Telegraph, in which he gamely discussed some of the controversy that has swirled since Weiss was appointed to her role last year. “In the U.S., the controversy has been framed as, ‘CBS News is becoming anti-woke’. But that’s not what Bari is about,” Phillip said. “She has her own views, some of which I’m sympathetic to, some of which I’m not, but her point is that the media should be heterodox. The interviews I’m interested in doing will include that group [of leaders].” “I’m not the smoothest presenter on television or reader of the autocue, but I guess they think that I manage the chaos [of live guests] well,” Phillips added. “Broadcast journalism has, to some extent, become the creature of entertainment. title: ‘Peaky Blinders’ Helps U.K. Region Land Official Production Hub Status From British Film Commission
full_text: Aug 3, 2026 2:51am PT ‘Peaky Blinders’ Helps U.K. Region Land Official Production Hub Status From British Film Commission By Alex Ritman Plus Icon Alex Ritman @alexritman Latest ‘Peaky Blinders’ Helps U.K. Region Land Official Production Hub Status From British Film Commission 2 hours ago Action Man Movie, Based on Iconic British Toy Originally Inspired by ‘G.I. Joe,’ in Development With Working Title and Hasbro 4 hours ago ‘The Inbetweeners’ Reunion Movie in the Works at Netflix With Original Lead Cast to Return 2 days ago See All ©Netflix/Courtesy Everett Collection “ Peaky Blinders ” may have given closely clipped back and sides haircuts a new lease of life, but it’s now helped a region of the U.K. land official backing as a center for high-end productions. The British Film Commission has announced that the West Midlands, home to the city of Birmingham and where “Peaky Blinders” is set and shot, has been named the U.K.’s eighth official regional production hub for scripted inward investment for film and high-end TV. Related Stories Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey’s ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Revival Delays Ticket Sales Until Fall Ariana Grande Sues Hackers for Leaking Unreleased Music and Footage According to the Commission, having served as production base for “Peaky Blinders,” the feature film “The Immortal Man” and the as-yet untitled “Peaky Blinders” spin-off series, the region has now fulfilled the criteria needed to receive official hub status. Popular on Variety The West Midlands joins South-West England (Bristol); North-West England (Manchester and Liverpool); Yorkshire (Leeds); Northern Ireland (Belfast); Scotland (Glasgow and Edinburgh); Wales (Cardiff); and London & South-East England as an official production hub, lending its strength to a UK-wide offer which contributed £5.8 billion ($7.8 billion) to the UK economy in 2025. “As Tommy Shelby of the Peaky Blinders once said, ‘when you plan something well, there’s no need to rush.’ The growing success of the West Midlands as a U.K. production hub certainly bears this out. Over the course of nearly 15 years, the region has steadily grown in strength and stature, building skills, infrastructure and reputation,” said Adrian Wootton, Chief Executive of the British Film Commission. “With the West Midlands becoming an official regional production hub, our offer to the global film and TV industry now spans the length and breadth of the U.K.: wherever you base your production, you’re within a stone’s throw of world-class facilities, crew and talent, with access to one-of-a-kind locations and some of the world’s most stable, transparent and generous tax incentives.” The two upcoming “Peaky Blinders” spin-off series are being film at the recently opened in Birmingham’s Digbeth Loc. Studios, which was founded by show creator Steven Knight . “I’m thrilled that the West Midlands has been recognised as a fantastic place to make film and TV,” said Knight. The opening of Digbeth Loc. Studios is an important part of that ambition, providing a home for world-class film and television production in the heart of Birmingham. We are at the beginning of a journey, and we’ve got off to a great start. The Stephen Sondheim revival, which also stars Grande’s “Wicked” co-star Jonathan Bailey , was scheduled to premiere at London’s Barbican next summer with producers set to launch ticket sales after Grande completed the last leg of her “The Eternal Sunshine Tour” on Sept. 1 in the U.K. Related Stories Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey’s ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Revival Delays Ticket Sales Until Fall 'Sunday in the Park with George' Producers Confirm Summer 2027 Show Will Go On 'As Planned' After Ariana Grande Exits However, on Sunday night reps for the actress said Grande will be “taking a step back from visibility” after she completes her tour — which includes dropping out of the play. Popular on Variety But the show must go on and a rep for producers Empire Street Productions tells Variety : “The production will open at the Barbican in summer 2027 as planned, and casting will be announced in due course.” Grande was set to star as both Dot and Marie in the revival opposite Bailey as painter George Seurat, offering “Wicked” fans a rare opportunity to see the film’s stars together live on stage. “Sunday in the Park With George” is directed by Tony and Olivier Award winner Marianne Elliot, with design by Tom Scutt. Auditions for the ensemble have been taking place in London this summer. Producers for the show said they “wish [Grande] nothing but the best,” adding: “We know this cannot have been an easy decision, and she makes it with our complete understanding and support.” In recent years fans have expressed increasing concern for Grande, particularly in regards to her physical appearance. title: In ‘Donkey Princess,’ a Young Royal Travels Through Worlds – and Film Genres – in Search of Love (Exclusive Trailer)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 3, 2026 2:30am 'Donkey Princess' film still Courtesy of Benjamin Echazarreta Cristóbal León and Joaquín Cociña, the Chilean filmmakers who have made a name for themselves with The Wolf House and The Hyperboreans , as well as collaborators of Ari Aster , will world premiere their third feature film, Donkey Princess ( Princesa Burro ), in the international competition program of the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival on Friday, Aug. 7. As was the case with their first two feature films, their new movie is an ambitious cinematic ride. And it comes in the form of an envelope-pushing fairy tale. Related Stories Movies Woody Harrelson to Receive Honorary Heart of Sarajevo at Bosnian Film Festival Movies Locarno Pro Takes on the Big Issues: AI, "Algorithms and Consolidation Versus Creative Freedom" The Donkey Princess focuses on Diana, the princess of an ancient kingdom, whose father, King Arthur, has forbidden love. That is why, when Diana falls in love with Lalo, the King simply banishes him. “Using a magical bracelet, Diana travels to other worlds in search of her love,” explains a synopsis. “Discovering that her father manipulates her decisions, she must face her fears and change her destiny.” The travels that Diana embarks on allow León and Cociña to use the places she visits as a way to explore different film periods and genres. “Diana travels through parallel worlds where each universe transforms the film’s genre,” the creative duo explains in a directors’ note on the Locarno website. “The film brings this constant mutation of realities into live action, where fantasy reshapes everything.” The cast is led by Antonia Giesen and also features Andrew Bargsted and Francisco Melo. Alejandra Moffat co-wrote the screenplay for Donkey Princess with the directors. The movie, featuring cinematography by Benjamín Echazarreta, was edited by Soledad Salfate, Maria Salazar, León and Cociña. Bendita Film Sales is handling international sales. “ Donkey Princess is our way of reimagining the history of fantasy cinema: a film that engages with this tradition while presenting our own vision of the genre,” León and Cociña highlight in a directors’ statement. “In The Wolf House , The Hyperboreans and in our short films, we have explored worlds where dreams and nightmares dominate the materiality of space, generating universes in constant construction, mutation and destruction. In Donkey Princess , we take these ideas and adapt them into a fiction feature film performed entirely by actors. The story is loosely inspired by the tale Donkeyskin , as recorded in writing by [Charles] Perrault and later adapted for the screen by Jacques Demy.” But there is really no way to get a feel for a film by León and Cociña other than to watch it. THR can now exclusively premiere a trailer for Donkey Princess . So, check it out right here – and get ready to have your mind blown. THR

title: Zee Shareholders Approve $330 Million Capital Raise Before Indian Regulator Bars Company From Markets
full_text: Aug 3, 2026 2:02am PT Zee Shareholders Approve $330 Million Capital Raise Before Indian Regulator Bars Company From Markets By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Zee Shareholders Approve $330 Million Capital Raise Before Indian Regulator Bars Company From Markets 3 hours ago Massive Attack Addresses Singapore Concert Aftermath in New Statement 5 hours ago Korea Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Captures 81% Market Share in Colossal Debut 6 hours ago See All ZEE Entertainment Enterprises Limited/Getty Images Shareholders of Indian media giant Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. approved a promoter group fund infusion worth INR3143.5 crore ($330 million) and a new employee stock option plan at an extraordinary general meeting, a day before India’s securities regulator barred the company and two of its top executives from the market. The Mumbai-headquartered media and technology company said its shareholders backed a preferential issue of 249,485,563 warrants to a promoter group entity, priced at INR126 ($1.32) each. A warrant gives its holder the right to convert it into a company share at a later date, at a price fixed now. Once exercised, the promoters’ stake will grow to 23.79% of the company. Related Stories Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey’s ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Revival Delays Ticket Sales Until Fall Ariana Grande to Take ‘Step Back From Visibility’ After Tour Ends Amid ‘Public Scrutiny,’ Drops Out of ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Musical Shareholders also cleared the “Truly Yours” employee stock option plan, under which 37,422,835 stock options with a face value of INR1 ($0.01) each will be granted to eligible employees of Zee and its subsidiaries, in one or more tranches. Popular on Variety R. Gopalan, chair of Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd., thanked shareholders for their support. “This approval is a clear reflection of the shareholders’ belief in the Company and its management,” Gopalan said. “The board firmly believes that robust growth capital coupled with enhanced promoter alignment, will serve as key enablers in ensuring long-term profitability in a dynamic business environment.” A day after the shareholder vote, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) – the country’s capital markets watchdog – issued an order barring Zee from the securities market for two months and barring chair emeritus Subhash Chandra and managing director and CEO Punit Goenka from the market for 12 months each. SEBI also imposed penalties totaling INR1.48 crore ($155,000), split between INR30 lakh ($31,000) on Zee, INR58 lakh ($61,000) on Goenka and INR60 lakh ($63,000) on Chandra. The order concerns the pledge of a Zee-owned property in Hyderabad, used in December 2018 to secure INR726 crore ($76.1 million) in loans for four entities linked to Essel Group, the promoter group associated with Chandra and Goenka. SEBI found the pledge was never disclosed to or approved by Zee’s board or audit committee, and determined that Chandra and Goenka had used the company’s asset to shield borrowings tied to their own family-controlled entities. A company spokesperson said Zee was reviewing the order with legal counsel and did not expect it to affect the fund-raising exercise. “The company would like to clarify that pursuant to the regulatory approvals received from the stock exchanges and from its esteemed shareholders at the Extraordinary General Meeting conducted on 31st July 2026, it will further take all required steps to successfully complete the fund-raising exercise, which is aimed at strengthening its financial foundation, and will also continue to work towards creating value for its stakeholders,” the spokesperson said. The order is the latest in a long-running SEBI probe into Zee’s promoters. The regulator first barred Goenka and Chandra from holding managerial or directorial roles at listed companies in June 2023, over allegations of fund diversion. The Securities Appellate Tribunal set aside that order that October, but the scrutiny continued to shadow Zee’s proposed $10 billion merger with Sony Pictures Networks India, which collapsed in January 2024 . Chandra later accused SEBI’s then-chair of scuttling the merger. In the two years since, Zee has cut roughly 15% of its workforce and expanded into sports broadcasting, striking a deal with FIFA in June for Indian broadcast and streaming rights to the 2026 and 2030 World Cups and 37 other tournaments through 2034. The newly approved capital is earmarked for that broader push, with the company directing the funds toward sports, acquisitions, digital content, artificial intelligence and microdrama through fiscal 2029, with sports receiving the largest share. title: Japan’s Wowow Reveals First-Look Of Six-Part Series Based On Riku Onda’s ‘The Aosawa Murders’, Starring Yukino Kishii
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' Opens To $355 Million U.S. & $927M Worldwide, Second Best Start Of All Time At Box Office Read the full story By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Singapore’s Wave Films Taps Former Cambodian Broadcasting Chief Dave Ulmer To Drive U.S. Expansion Mouly Surya, Reza Rahadian & Prasanna Vithanage Among Filmmakers Selected For Busan’s Asian Project Market Korean Box Office Up 42% In 2026 H1, Driven By ‘The King’s Warden’ & Other Local Hits; ‘Project Hail Mary’ Tops Imports View All August 3, 2026 1:49am Yukino Kishii plays the character Makiko in her 20s & 40s Wowow EXCLUSIVE: Japanese broadcaster Wowow has announced that it’s producing a live-action series based on Riku Onda’s best-selling mystery novel The Aosawa Murders (Eugenia) , set to star Yukino Kishii , known internationally for her role in recent Cannes title All The Lovers In The Night . The six-episode series is scripted by Naoko Adachi ( What Did You Eat Yesterda y?) with Go Furukawa ( Kaneko’s Commissary ) as lead director. Hayato Kawai, whose credits include Disney+ series Gannibal , also directs. The series will premiere on Sunday, November 8, airing and streaming weekly on Wowow. Related Stories News Anne Watanabe & Jasper Pääkkönen To Lead Japanese-Nordic Noir Series 'Blood & Sweat' For Wowow, Nelonen, ICS Nordic & Boat Rocker Studios News 'Bye Bye, Earth' Anime Will Be Joint Production By Sony Pictures Japan, Crunchyroll, Wowow The story opens with a mass poisoning at the home of a prominent family in a Japanese coastal city and follows the impact of the event on a novelist, who was among the first at the scene and later wrote a book about the case; a blind girl who was the family’s sole survivor; and a writer investigating the case. Watch on Deadline Yukino Kishii, in her first role for Wowow, plays the role of Makiko Saiga – a woman who witnessed the mass poisoning at the age of eleven and later wrote a novel about it – and who freely changes her voice and manner of speaking depending on whom she is talking to Wowow has also revealed first-look photos of Kishii in this challenging role (see above) – showing her playing the character in two different time periods: in the 1980s when as a twenty-something Makiko went from door to door listening to the people whose lives the case had upended; and in the 2000s, now in her forties, when she is confronted about the truth of the case by a freelance writer. In addition to All The Lovers In The Nigh t, which premiered in Cannes Un Certain Regard and has sold widely internationally, Kishii’s credits include Small, Slow But Steady (2022) – for which she won several acting honours including Best Actress at the Japan Academy Film Prize – and Japan-Taiwan co-production Sinsin And The Mouse . Kishii commented on her casting in the series: “I had been reading Onda-sensei’s novels since junior high school, so the offer made me very happy – and put just as much pressure on me. When I heard the scripts would be by Naoko Adachi, who always renders the world from so many angles, I felt that with her I might be able to dive into this story.” Published in English as The Aosawa Murders , Onda’s 2005 novel Eugenia won the 59th Mystery Writers of Japan Award for Best Novel, and has sold a cumulative 380,000 copies in Japan. The novel has been translated into six languages (English, German, French, Spanish, Italian and Korean) and was selected as a New York Times Notable Book of 2020; featured among The Guardian’s best recent crime and thrillers of 2020; and won first place in the international category of the German Crime Fiction Prize in 2022. Naoko Adachi, who has adapted the novel, is one of Japan’s most highly regarded screenwriters. In addition to TV Tokyo hit series What Did You Eat Yesterday? , her credits also include NHK morning drama Welcome Home, Mone and upcoming historical drama Gyakuzoku no Bakushin . She also previously worked with Kishii on NHK’s Farewell Hospital (2024) and Farewell Hospital 2 (2026). Takeo Kodera, a producer for Kadokawa, which published the original Japanese version of the novel, brought the project to Wowow, which produced with the cooperation of Kadokawa Daiei Studio. Masaki Yamada, Chief Producer at the Drama Production Department of Wowow’s Content Production Division, said he was attracted to the work because: “The question is not ‘who did it?’ but ‘why do people go on being driven mad and damaged by this case?’’ — and there is that sense that the reader is somehow participating in the story.” Commenting on the adaptation, Onda said: “Since publication in 2005 I had received many offers to adapt the novel, including from overseas, so for the adaptation to be decided in the book’s 20th-anniversary year – just as the complete edition was published – is deeply moving.” Adachi commented: “I feel Eugenia is a story that drags readers and viewers out of the safe seat of the ‘bystander’. You are pulled into the case whether you like it or not, and as the story goes on you can no longer say for certain that what you saw is the truth exactly as you saw it.” Wowow is handling international rights to the series and will be presenting it to buyers at the upcoming TIFFCOM and ATF markets in Tokyo and Singapore later this year. Harrelson will receive the festival’s Honorary Heart of Sarajevo Award in recognition of his outstanding contribution to the film industry and acting career, following in the footsteps of recent recipients such as Stellan Skarsgård, Paolo Sorrentino, Meg Ryan, Alexander Payne and Lynne Ramsay. “Woody Harrelson is one of those actors you believe in even in the most improbable roles, while at the same time you can easily imagine him as someone you might spend time with every day,” said Sarajevo director Jovan Marjanović. Related Stories Festivals Diego Luna To Receive Honorary Heart Of Sarajevo Award Festivals Sarajevo Film Festival Unveils Full Competition Lineup “That remarkable ease of performance is, in fact, one of the hardest qualities to achieve on screen, yet he delivers it film after film. His talent, charisma, and boldness serve as an inspiration to many future generations. It is our great honor to present him with the Honorary Heart of Sarajevo.” Watch on Deadline Harrelson has historic links to the festival as co-star of Michael Winterbottom’s 1997 film Welcome to Sarajevo , which premiered at Cannes and then also screened at the 3rd Sarajevo Film Festival, less than two years after the end of the siege of the city. The film – a powerful examination of war in Bosnia in the mid-1990s and the role of journalists in its media coverage – will screen in the festival once again as part of the open air programme. Harrelson played ego-driven American reporter Jimmy Flynn. Harrelson has earned three Academy Award nominations, including Best Actor for The People vs. Larry Flynt and Best Supporting Actor for The Messenger and Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri , and starred in Ruben Östlund’s Palme d’Or winner Triangle of Sadness . He next leads Apple TV’s Brothers alongside Matthew McConaughey, premiering September 23, and stars opposite Kristen Stewart in Quentin Dupieux’s Full Phil , which premiered at Cannes this year. He recently wrapped Netflix’s The Cackling of the Dodos with Sam Rockwell and is producing a documentary on Austin’s iconic Armadillo World Headquarters. Harrelson wrote, directed and starred in Lost in London , the first feature film shot in a single continuous take and broadcast live to theaters. An Emmy Award winner for his iconic portrayal of Woody Boyd on Cheers , his television credits also include True Detective and The White House Plumbers . He has also distinguished himself on stage as an actor, writer and director, starring in the Broadway revival of The Rainmaker , the West End’s On An Average Day and Night of the Iguana , and directing his own off Broadway production Bullet for Adolf , which he cowrote with Frankie Hyman. In other Sarajevo news, the festival announced over the weekend that it will also be laying on a special 25th anniversary screening of a restored 4K version of Danis Tanovíc’s 2001 Oscar-winning feature No Man’s Land exploring the absurdity of war through the prism of the Bosnian War. The Sarajevo Film Festival runs from August 14 to 21. title: Erik Poppe’s ‘Beloved’ to Open Haugesund: ‘All Eyes Are on Norway,’ Says Festival Chief Tonje Hardersen
full_text: Aug 3, 2026 1:00am PT Erik Poppe’s ‘Beloved’ to Open Haugesund: ‘All Eyes Are on Norway,’ Says Festival Chief Tonje Hardersen Cristian Mungiu, Nikolaj Coster-Waldau and Anders Danielsen Lie are some of the star names attending the Norwegian Int. Film Festival at Haugesund By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest Erik Poppe’s ‘Beloved’ to Open Haugesund: ‘All Eyes Are on Norway,’ Says Festival Chief Tonje Hardersen 4 hours ago DR Sales Closes With WDR/Arte, VRT, NRK in Multi Buyers Pact on Norwegian Wildlife Doc ‘Frost Without Snow and Ice’ (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago U.K. Heavyweight Doc Player Jane Ray Boards Argentina’s ‘The Nights’ by Ana Bovino Ahead of ECAM Forum (EXCLUSIVE) 2 months ago See All Credit: Helge Skodvin, Paradox, SF Studios After the World Cup where Norway made a splash with its wealth of soccer talent – led by Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard – the Nordic nation will be showcasing some of its biggest film talents at the 54 th edition of the Norwegian International Film Festival in Haugesund, running Aug. 22-28. Out of 84 feature length and 20 short films in the program, 22 Norwegian features and 15 shorts made the cut, including “ Beloved ” (“Kjærast”) by acclaimed Oscar-shortlisted Erik Poppe (“The Kings Choice,” “A Thousand Times Goodnight,” “ The Emigrants ”). The drama, repped internationally by Reinvent Yellow , will have its world premiere in the picturesque Norwegian coast town Aug. 23, as its opening film. Based on the only original screenplay by Nobel Prize-winning author Jon Fosse, the film stars Leo Magnus de la Nuez (“Beforeigners”) and Kristi-Helene Giæver Engeberg (“War Sailor”) as Asle and Gerd, who live an idyllic life with their son in a small Norwegian coastal town. But soon their perfect love is put to test, as Asle, a sailor, is inexorably drawn by the call of the sea. Related Stories Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey’s ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Revival Delays Ticket Sales Until Fall Ariana Grande Sues Hackers for Leaking Unreleased Music and Footage Festival director Tonje Hardersen said “Beloved’ is the perfect opener. “Poppe opened the festival two years ago with “ Quisling – The Final Days ;” he’s a true Haugesund regular, and Jon Fosse was actually born in Haugesund, so we’re thrilled to have them with us with a powerful film, set in the dazzlingly beautiful Western Norwegian landscape.” Popular on Variety “Beloved” is a love story full of the unspoken, tenderness, and mystery, unmistakably Jon Fosse,” said Poppe before adding: “We live in a time where much of what we see on film and series depicts cynicism and human distance. Perhaps the most radical thing we can do now is to tell stories about closeness and hope.” The pic is produced by Poppe’s regular partner Finn Gjerdrum of SF Studios ’ banner Paradox. Another hotly anticipated new Norwegian film, picked for the closing gala, is “The Murder of Benjamin,” based on the real-life murder of Benjamin Hermansen, a 15-year-old boy of mixed Norwegian and Malian heritage, who was brutally murdered by a neo-Nazi in 2001. Repped by TrustNordisk , the drama is helmed by Ingvild Søderlind, credited for Netflix’ “Royalteen: Princess Margrethe” and “Battle: Frestyle.” Seasoned Thomas Robsahm (“The Worst Person in the World,” “Lovable”) produces for Nordisk Film Production Norway. “It’s a strong film that follows the dramatic racially-motivated murder that happened 25 years ago. For me it was yesterday, but the younger generation doesn’t know about it which is why it’s key to highlight it at Haugesund,” said Hardersen. Cracks in Norwegian society The festival chief noted that cracks in Norwegian society is a predominant theme this year, tackled as well in Jørgen Nordby’s Norwegian doc-feature “The Voice That Vanished,” a world premiere. The pic follows local artist Helene Bøksle and the traumatic experience of having her vocals from the game “ Age of Conan” used by the July 22, 2011 mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik in his propaganda videos. Then in Cristian Mungiu ’s Palme d’Or winner “Fjord,” one of a handful Cannes competition entries secured by Hardersen (with “Fatherland,” “Parallel Tales” and “The Beloved”), it’s the turn of Norway’s child protection system to come in for scrutiny. “I’m really curious to see how the film will go down at the very first screening with a national audience,” said Hardersen. Mungiu will walk the Haugesund red carpet Aug. 25, when his Cannes winner opens New Nordic Films, the festival’s industry sidebar and biggest Nordic Film Market of the year, together with the twin event Nordic Film Market at Göteborg. As underscored by the fest honcho, “Fjord” stars Renate Reinsve who toplines Haugesund’s other local pick “ Butterfly ” by Itonje Søimer Guttormsen, and the Oscar winner “Sentimental Value.” Screening at the Amanda Nominees sidebar, Joachim Trier’s family drama has a chance to make history at the Norway’s Amanda national film awards if he coverts all its 12 nods into wins Aug. 22 at Haugesund’s Festiviteten Concert Hall. Besides Mungiu, A-list talent expected take in “Game of Thrones”’ Nikolaj Coster-Waldau , a producer together with Norway’s Kristian Landmark on the Greenlandic-set documentary “Qajaq Man,” and local household name Anders Danielsen Lie (“The Worst Person in the World”), whose performance as jazz legend Bill Evans in the Berlin Silver Bear winner “ Everybody Digs Bill Evans ” enthused critics, including Variety’s . Danielsen Lie will be honored at Haugesund alongside film and theatre actress Anne Marie Ottesen, when their names will be added to the festival’s Walk of Fame at a ceremony Aug. 22. Among the festival’s top non-competitive sections, the Nordic Focus will screen 10 new titles including Finnish chiller “Nightborn” and Danish gothic gay romance “ No Rest for the Wicked ” which scooped two top awards each at the recent Fantasia Film Fest; Haugesund’s parallel children’s festival Cinemagi will open with the Norwegian kids movie “Back To Tottori,” sequel to Silje Salomonsen and Arild Østin Ommundsen’s 2021 Amanda winner “Sisters: The Summer We Found Our Superpowers.” All Eyes on Norway “Our cinema is strong, and after the World Cup, all eyes are on Norway. We’re enjoying a unique momentum with which to further boost our films and country as a film nation. However, our audiovisual sector as a whole is still struggling, with many people losing their jobs,” commented Hardersen, who said the topic of how to strengthen the Norwegian industry in the next decade will be one of the main themes of Haugesund’s Film Policy Conference on Aug. 23. “We’re not part of the E.U. and don’t want to be left out when the E.U. launches its flagship [2028-2034] AgoraEU program,” she said. As for the Norwegian International Film Festival which she has headed since 2015, Hardersen is pleased to announce that it has consolidated its brand in 2026 by expanding its footprint to Stavanger, the Rogaland region’s largest city and Norway’s oil capital. The Stavanger Festival’s soft launch last March sold more than 10,000 tickets and boosted the Norwegian International Film Festival’s overall visitors by 30%. “As Stavanger’s first film festival, we tapped into the large expat community working in the oil business and university students. It was a great experience,” said Hardersen. “Government support to our festival is based on our ability to renew ourselves, and the Stavanger film event was also a way to give back to our key backer, the Rogaland County.” Would she be tempted in the future to move the must-attend industry showcase New Nordic Films to Stavanger, four times the size of Haugesund? “No”, she said. “The beauty and uniqueness of Haugesund is its small size. The band said its members were “detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned” following the show, and described some members undergoing hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation as part of the process. The band said the “Free Palestine” chants heard at the concert arose spontaneously from the audience, both before the performance and again at its close, and noted they had understood the flag they displayed to represent “a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries.” The group expressed appreciation for the warmth of Singaporean fans and voiced hope that citizens there would in future be able to express their views freely. The statement closed: “As we were saying … Free Palestine.” Related Stories Ariana Grande and Jonathan Bailey’s ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Revival Delays Ticket Sales Until Fall Ariana Grande to Take ‘Step Back From Visibility’ After Tour Ends Amid ‘Public Scrutiny,’ Drops Out of ‘Sunday in the Park With George’ Musical PREVIOUSLY: The two founder members of Massive Attack have been permanently barred from re-entering Singapore after unfurling a Palestinian flag during the British trip-hop group’s concert in the city-state, according to a joint statement from the Singapore Police Force and the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA). Popular on Variety The statement said police investigated both band members for “their actions of support for a political cause and unfurling of a foreign flag” during the show at The Star Theatre on July 29. Following the investigation, and in consultation with the Attorney-General’s Chambers, police administered stern warnings to both men for offences under Section 3 of the Foreign National Emblems (Control of Display) Act 1949 and Section 16 of the Public Order Act. “Both men will also be banned from re-entering Singapore,” the statement said. According to the statement, the event organizer had acknowledged the licensing conditions attached to the concert beforehand, but both band members held up a “foreign flag” onstage during the performance, with one shouting “Free Palestine.” The IMDA said it is investigating a possible breach of several licence conditions, including one barring performers from displaying flags tied to any cause, and will act once that inquiry concludes. The regulator added it will not approve any future application for the band to perform in Singapore given the entry ban. The concert was the band’s only scheduled Singapore date on its current tour, with video of the flag display circulating widely online alongside footage of the crowd joining in chants of “Free Palestine.” The two men are Massive Attack’s founding members, Robert “3D” Del Naja and Grant “Daddy G” Marshall, who make up its current touring lineup; authorities did not name them in the statement. Singapore maintains strict rules on the public display of foreign flags and emblems without a permit, framing the laws as necessary to protect the country’s racial and religious harmony. The joint statement reiterated that position, with authorities saying they “take a serious view of acts which could potentially harm the racial and religious harmony in Singapore” and urging the public, including foreigners, “to refrain from importing foreign politics” into the country. “The peace and harmony between different races and religions in Singapore should not be taken for granted, and we must not let external events affect our society,” the statement said. Massive Attack has been among the more vocal acts in music in its support for Palestinian causes. title: Locarno Pro Takes on the Big Issues: AI, “Algorithms and Consolidation Versus Creative Freedom”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 3, 2026 12:01am Markus Duffner Courtesy of Locarno Film Festival Locarno is not “just” about the discovery of new film gems and the celebration of the art of cinema. It’s also about discussing and conducting business, about addressing the challenges facing the industry and about networking to enable all of that. So, while people can explore new and classic cinema during the 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival , running Aug. 5-15, the Swiss fest’s Locarno Pro industry program returns with a spotlight on the big issues of the day and the future, along with much more, during its 15th edition, taking place Aug. 6-11. Related Stories Movies 'The Days Off' Is a "Love Letter to That Internet That No Longer Quite Exists" (Locarno Trailer) TV Scott Hylands, Star of TV's 'Night Heat' on Both Sides of the Border, Dies at 83 The 2026 program of panels and keynotes will kick off with the traditional StepIn session, which will this year explore how power structures, politics, AI and data are reshaping independent cinema. Also returning is Open Doors, the co-production platform and talent development program for filmmakers from regions where artistic expression is at risk. After all, Locarno Pro also sees itself as a talent incubation and training platform. This year marks the second year with a f ocus on Africa , with the spotlight being put on six projects in development, six producers and five directors. Plus, in partnership with ACAU – Agencia del Cine y el Audiovisual del Uruguay, L ocarno Pro’s First Look initiative for works-in-progress will showcase six Uruguayan films currently in post-production. The networking platform Match Me! and co-development program Alliance 4 Development also return, as do the classic film program Locarno Heritage and programs targeting young industry professionals in the U30 think tank. Among the innovations this year is the launch of a Locarno Pro podcast and the inaugural Open Doors Connect program, which “allows foundations, film institutions, and organizations to join by sponsoring an industry professional, opening up new financing models, markets, and collaborations rooted in global equality.” Markus Duffner , director of Locarno Pro in his sixth year, expects around 2,000 accredited industry guests to attend this year, with around three-quarters of those coming from Europe. Among the attendees are an estimated 800 producers, 350 buyers, about 100 sales agents and 300 film festival programmers. Ahead of all the debates and networking, Duffner took time to talk to THR about the return of the Locarno Investment Community for its second year, the choice of Uruguay, the hot issues in focus and why AI will be touched on throughout the program. After its debut last year, the Locarno Investment Community is back for its second edition. Why does this offering make so much sense, and what was the experience and feedback like last year? In the first year of the investment community, we had about 40 private investors of different profiles – from private banks to philanthropic organizations, mostly from North America. Then there were European funds that are investing not only in projects but also in companies and slates. And there were also private individuals who are curious about how to invest in culture and in film in particular. We organize this in partnership with Oxbelly, which is developing talented scriptwriters, but also bringing in their ambassadors and philanthropic investors from the U.S. So, we created the program together, and last year, it was like the pilot edition with some closed-door sessions. For this year’s second edition of the Locarno Investment Community, we will have around 45 investment players coming, and we will have a stronger program for them to also network and mingle with our talent. It’s an added value for both the Swiss industry and for the European industry in Locarno. So, I think it’s something that’s here to stay for us. Are any participants from last year returning or are they all new? I would say 25 percent are coming back, and then we have added new layers. It will also always depend on the films that are selected for the festival. We’re different from Sundance Catalyst or the Cannes Investorx Circle . We are really an informal platform. We create networking opportunities with all the lunches, one-to-one meetings and closed-door sessions, which are useful for both networking reasons, but also for training, education and mentoring for both the investors and our talent. And everything in Locarno Pro is tailor-made and custom-made based on the profile of the people who are coming, so that we don’t waste anyone’s time. We think about who sits where at which table at lunch or why this person should meet with that person. Once you get to Locarno, we take care of you, and that’s unique. And innovation is key. It’s not copy-paste. We stop and look at what our industry needs. The idea is to innovate our Locarno Pro platform because of the state of the traditional financing system. Everybody is worried about what’s going to happen in the future. This year continues that. Tell me some more about those future concerns, please. There are some earthquakes that are shaking up the infrastructure of the global industry. Let’s see what happens with the merger of Paramount and Warner. Let’s see what happens with everything that AI can do, as groundbreaking technologies will change the industry. I’m not even talking about generative AI and the creative element, but what’s happening in the industry with those tools. Innovation is important for us. And for us, innovation is also about bringing new players to our platform. It’s our duty to offer new options to talents, filmmakers and producers. How do the connections you enable lead to results? We are pretty realistic. It’s not that the connections we create are leading to immediate results, but our incubation works, and we have some success stories, such as Flow , the Oscar-winning animation . This year, we also won a Silver Bear in Berlin [for best screenplay] with Nina Roza , which was one of our first-look works-in-progress from Canada last year. In the Piazza Grande program this year, we have a film called The Chilean , which is co-produced by an Italian and a Chilean producer who met in 2017 in Locarno in our Match Me! [networking offering]. They even got a small grant from Ticino [which is the Swiss region that Locarno is part of] and got to shoot a few days in Locarno, so for me this is like the perfect story to show how Locarno Pro plays a role. Probably, this film wouldn’t have been made if it wasn’t for the platform we created. How does Locarno fit into the annual schedule for film investors? Investors either have funds, mostly smaller funds, or they can allocate $1 million a year, and they come to Locarno looking at the festival calendar. They have Venice and Toronto coming up, and then they have a few other smaller markets for potentially another $400,000 or so to invest. If you invest $100,000-$150,000 in each film, you’re scouting for projects. And there are some funds that need to spend their money by the end of the year. So for them to come to Locarno increases the potential for them to find a project. If we have 85 talents, and we match them based on their profile, there is a good chance. Uruguay is the focus of this year’s first look works-in-progress showcase at Locarno Pro. How did you choose the country? What we do when choosing a country is secure a partnership with a local institution to allow us to get the full picture of every country. And we work with this local partner a year in advance, or even a year and a half in advance. When we chose a focus on Spain, we were looking at post-COVID politics, and saw that the Spanish government invested so much money into cultural recovery after COVID that we thought, let’s do something with Spain. Within a couple of years, they must have a boom in projects and a lot of good films with commercial and festival potential. Similarly, if you look at the Latin American landscape, given the current political situation in Argentina, I think Uruguay and Brazil now are the two thriving countries that are able to invest a lot in minority co-productions as well as majority co-productions. They have a very thriving industry at the moment. Uruguay, especially if you look at its proximity to Argentina and how it can compensate for that, is really interesting. And in talking with ACAU – Agencia del Cine y el Audiovisual del Uruguay, we felt this is a really good moment to focus on Uruguay. This year’s six works-in-progress from Uruguay are a really diverse selection in terms of genres, in terms of geographical regions and in the way they are shot. They provide a really nice picture of Uruguay today. In this year’s Locarno Pro panel discussions and keynotes, what are some of the key overarching themes? We’re having over 50 speakers this year. StepIn, which is our thought-provoking kick-off event every year, [film industry data analyst] Stephen Follows is going to talk about our main topics, which will be reflected across the rest of the Locarno Pro program, which is: “Power. People. Data.” – and the future of them. He will address “Fear, Lies, and the Illusion of Control.” We were thinking of our core themes even before the [Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery] merger news, and then we said: “Okay, this is a question of power, of course, but at the same time, it’s a question of the algorithm, so data.” There is subscription fatigue or fatigue of the algorithmization of products and content that is available not only online but also in cinemas nowadays. Tell me a bit more about that and other themes! Studios use algorithms to decide what to finance, to develop, and all that. Stephen Follows has been vocal about this. But for us, he will do a special intro. Our program will also focus on gender equality nowadays in the industry and what it means to distribute a film today. And, of course, how to finance them will be a topic. We’ll talk about films versus formula – algorithms and consolidation versus creative freedom. That is not AI per se, but there is a lot of AI in there. We will think a lot about why cinema still matters and what it means to release a film. There is a little bit of activism in it, but we can see that fewer films are doing huge box office, and others are flopping, so this is a market trend that has been changing. This year, we’ll also talk about the cost of inclusion. Who can afford to be in this industry? Things are changing so fast. Our ambition is not to find a solution, but to look at risk and opportunity, and maybe anticipate the market trends ahead. But the time horizons have changed. Before the pandemic, StepIn was aiming at five-year predictions. Now, the industry is moving so fast, with all the tech disruption, the market and all the politics, that if we can predict what happens next year or in two years, I would say we are doing a good job. For the first time, we will also do a podcast of about an hour with the topics in focus. And AI will be a topic across the Locarno Pro sessions and events? On all [panels and sessions], more or less, there is at least one person who is thinking about and covering AI. Everything is influenced by AI these days, including financing, distribution and sales. And since there is no legislation yet on a European level to create precise rules, so we want to allow for conversation and dialogue. We invite policymakers and members of film institutes too, who can then relate takeaways to their ministries of culture or the European Parliament so they understand what key players are going through. Film restorations have also been a key part of Locarno Pro… Yes, we have a full-day Heritage Monday dedicated to new restorations we present. We restore two films a year. This year, it was a Senegalese film from Safi Faye, Letter From My Village , and Dances With Wolves , the Academy Award winner by Kevin Costner, which will be shown in a second screening in the Piazza Grande on Friday night. Restoration really goes to what Locarno’s mission is, including finding new audiences for classic films and giving them a new commercial life. THR

title: John Oliver Says Taco Bell Has the Moral High Ground Over Trump Administration Amid “Explosive Diarrhea” Parasite Crisis
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All August 2, 2026 9:59pm 'Last Week Tonight With John Oliver' Courtesy of HBO As four more U.S. states saw a breakout in cyclospora cases, linked to contaminated lettuce, John Oliver decided to weigh in on the parasite causing “debilitating explosive diarrhea” across the country. A total of nine states have now reported cases of cyclospora, which has been attributed to shredded iceberg lettuce sources by Taylor Farms. And according to recent data, almost 2,000 people in those states got sick after consuming the lettuce at a Taco Bell restaurant. Overall, it’s estimated that there are nearly 12,000 cases, with that number expected to grow. Related Stories TV John Oliver Talks New "Prospective Business Daddies" and Colbert Support Group and Reveals HBO Contract Extension (Exclusive) TV David Jenkins' 'Booster Gold' DC Series Not Moving Forward at HBO On Sunday’s Last Week Tonight , Oliver played a news clip in which the reporter advised viewers dining at a restaurant to “ask the source of their lettuce or … eat cooked vegetables instead” to avoid getting sick. Responded Oliver: “Yeah, the best advice they have for you right now is to basically play lettuce detective at every restaurant. And what are you really expecting them to say? ‘Oh shit, we actually get it from Sam’s Parasite Barn. We were hoping no one would ask.’ ‘Cause let’s be honest, your server doesn’t know where the restaurant sources their lettuce. Their main concern is that the bartender they fucked last week stopped working Mondays, and their manager won’t release next month’s schedule unless everyone goes to a poetry night, so why not give them all a break and just order soup.” Oliver then played another news clip in which the reporter said the symptoms include “debilitating, explosive diarrhea” that can last for weeks. The new clips also featured three people who had the illness describing their pain as “unbearable” and “horrible.” One noted that some folks are hoping to get the parasite to lose weight: “No, you don’t,” she said. Noted Oliver “Of course you don’t. Nobody should be looking at the people who pooped so weird that they made it onto the news and think, ‘It should have been me.'” Citing another news report, Oliver quoted an epidemiologist who described the illness’ symptoms as “uncontrollable and it’s very liquid. If you’ve seen pictures from cholera wars where the patients are on gurneys and the gurney has a hole where your butt goes and there’s a bucket underneath the hole, it’s very similar.” Said Oliver: “No offense, but I don’t think that epidemiologist should be allowed to give statements anymore. We were looking for something like, ‘It’ll cause digestive issues,’ not ‘Taco Bell made American shit so hard and wet they need assless beds like a 19th century poop ward.'” As Taco Bell sales dropped, the company put out a statement to reassure consumers: “We want you to hear it from us. We take your health and safety seriously and have removed all affected Taylor Farms lettuce from Taco Bell stores. So go ahead and enjoy your Taco Bell today. You always got us. We always got you. See you in the drive-through.” “No, you fucking won’t,” Oliver quipped. Oliver did give credit to Taco Bell for at least addressing the problem, while then turning to President Donald Trump and U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for creating a situation wherein authorities are not able to respond as effectively as in years past. He noted that the Food and Drug Administration “has been underfunded for decades now,” but under the Trump administration, the FDA has lost 20 percent of its staff, and the Centers for Disease Control has lost 25 percent of its staff, including eight of its 11 scientists who track food parasites. “Wait, only three people now?” Oliver asked. “That is clearly not enough. It really feels like we shouldn’t be able to fit the CDC’s entire parasite tracking team comfortably onto a porch glider.” Oliver noted that the day after Kennedy said the crisis was under control, the FDA announced it was investigating a new outbreak. “It does say something pretty grim about America, that when it comes to acting swiftly to prevent a public health threat, the current government just lost the moral high ground to fucking Taco Bell,” Oliver quipped. The Last Week Tonight host ended the segment with a parody ad for Taco Bell that started: “Hey America, we at Taco Bell want you to know we care about your health and safety.” It continued: “We know that because of our food, many of you have been shitting your brains out in a way that we never intended because Taco Bell’s always prided itself on two things: having the wettest food in America and only giving you the regular normal level of diarrhea. That’s why we’ve temporarily removed lettuce from our food, so while you’re powering through our Mexican food adjacent menu, including our, oh Jesus Christ, Sausage Crunchwrap Supreme, you can feel confident that you’re avoiding one narrow definition of gastrointestinal disease. Again, we’re not promising you won’t get regular diarrhea from it. And you’ve seen our food, right? There’s something on the menu called Diablo Dusted Chicken Nuggets, OK? We’re just saying, we’ll try not to give you the kind of diarrhea that’ll put you on the news.” THR
